evidence_level: suggestive (one quasi-experiment meeting WWC standards with reservations, one same-city fixed-effects study; no randomized trial)
pathway: A partnership between museums, zoos, botanical gardens or science centers and middle schools gives science teachers long-term professional development at the institutions, field trips for classes and free visit vouchers for families; students in these schools score a little higher on the grade 8 state science test.
model_match: Informal science institution partnership with schools in the Urban Advantage form: 100 or more hours of teacher professional development at the institution over several years, funded class field trips, family visit vouchers, and classroom science resources, for grade 6-8 science. A partner coded Y1.4 that runs stand-alone enrichment or a single field trip gets only the field-trip size, and a partner without school science teachers in the model gets no evidence level from this link.
typical_effect: WWC-extracted g = 0.06 on the New York State grade 8 science exam (Urban Advantage). At 0.06 standard deviations, roughly 2 more students in 100 reach proficient (normal approximation; District grade 8 science base rate not checked). Field trips alone: small positive effect on grade 8 science scores and proficiency (size to be confirmed).
caveats: One city (New York), one research group (NYU IESP) for both studies, so not independent replications; school-level participation, not random; the field-trip study overlaps the Urban Advantage schools. Outcome is the New York grade 8 science test, not the PSSA grade 4 or 8 science test. No evidence for grade 4. A Philadelphia analogue would need the District as co-partner (teacher time). Bounded by the Design2Learn after-school science null (T-P03).
rationale: S9 had no tested link. This is the most credible partner-shaped model found with a state science test as the outcome. The 2013 working paper also reports some evidence of higher high school science exam passing, which is the closest lead to S11 found anywhere (see T-P08). NURTURES (S-0191, S-0190: Ohio grade 5 science g = 0.08 after teacher professional development plus family science packs) is a similar teacher-PD lead, not relied on here. A 2025 Urban Advantage study (ERIC EJ1467585) found lower science-teacher turnover, which bears on A1.3 retention, not teacher attendance.

evidence_level: suggestive (two independent grantee quasi-experiments in Tennessee; no randomized trial; the one after-school science RCT was null)
pathway: Hands-on STEM camps during school breaks or extended-learning STEM projects outside regular classes, built around the science standards, go with higher scores on the state science test for elementary and middle school participants in matched comparisons.
model_match: A structured, standards-aligned, hands-on STEM camp or extended-learning program with multiple days of contact (Gear Up 4 STEM: school-break camps for grades 3-5; G2ROW STEM: multi-year project-based extended learning for middle school). Drop-in STEM clubs, single events and interest-only programs get no evidence level from this link.
typical_effect: G2ROW STEM: TNReady science g = 0.32 (and math 0.40) after up to three years, about one-third of a standard deviation (7 NCE points). Gear Up 4 STEM: significantly higher TNReady science scores in the year of attendance (size to be confirmed). Plan on the low end: both are grantee evaluations, and the after-school science RCT found no effect.
caveats: Both studies are quasi-experiments commissioned by the grantee or district, with self-selection into the program; baseline equivalence and effect size for Gear Up 4 STEM need checking. Tennessee test, not PSSA. Gear Up 4 STEM did not change school attendance. Bounded by the Design2Learn randomized null (T-P03), the New York Sun Works null in the multilevel model (T-P04) and the Massachusetts expanded learning time science result (T-013, if null). The existing Girlstart row (L-48) stays not recommended.
rationale: Two independent positive matched comparisons on the state science test move this above the old Girlstart-only evidence (L-48). Weight is limited by design and source; at most suggestive. If the checker finds no baseline equivalence for Gear Up 4 STEM, this rests on G2ROW alone and should be demoted to not recommended.

pathway: An after-school design-based science program that bridged school-day science with after-school activities did not change students' science interest, attendance or science grades in a randomized trial.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit. Tested model: Design2Learn (ExpandED Schools with the New York Hall of Science), co-taught by a school science teacher and after-school educators.
typical_effect: No substantial difference from control after-school programs; exposure was low.
caveats: Outcome is science course grades, not the state science test; the trial reported the control programs already offered science, and dosage was low. It is still the only randomized test of an after-school science model found.
rationale: Records the null that bounds T-P01 and T-P02: an after-school science program with good design features did not move science outcomes at the dosage delivered.

evidence_level: below bar or null on the state test
pathway: School gardens, hydroponic gardening and watershed field experiences have not been shown to raise state science test scores; the one randomized trial used a short researcher questionnaire and found very modest gains.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: Garden RCT: very modest gains on a 7-item researcher measure. Hydroponic program: non-significant in the multilevel model on the New York grade 4 science test. Pennsylvania watershed study: significant raw PSSA difference with no baseline adjustment.
caveats: No study with a state science test outcome met the bar. The reviews (Williams & Dixon 2013; Berezowitz et al. 2015) summarise mostly weak designs and are not meta-analyses.
rationale: Gardening and environmental education are common partner programs; this row tells partners not to claim PSSA science gains from them. Mason & Wendt is one of very few studies with PSSA science as the outcome of an enrichment program.

pathway: Text messages prompting parents to talk with children about science did not change science test scores and crowded out other parent engagement.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No detectable effect on science test scores.
caveats: England, not the United States; the crowd-out finding warns against stacking parent asks.
rationale: A low-cost family nudge partners might consider; the evidence says it does not move science scores.

proposed_tier: keep tier; add S9 as a smaller, less certain effect
evidence_level: B for universal school-day programs (unchanged); science outcome from fewer studies
pathway: Universal social and emotional learning curricula taught during the school day raise students' test scores slightly, including science scores in the studies that measured them.
model_match: Unchanged from L-13 (named structured SEL curriculum taught to whole classes during the school day).
typical_effect: Science: about +0.19 in Corcoran et al. (2018), shrinking in rigorous large trials; 0.06 in Zhao & Sang (2025). Plan on the smaller size.
caveats: Few studies measured science; neither meta-analysis used the PSSA science test. Add to caveats that science effects are smaller and less certain than reading and math.
rationale: Only research base touching S9 at meta-analytic level. Adds S9 to the indicator list with an explicit smaller-size caveat rather than a new link.

model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
caveats: Replace the S9 caveat: S9 now has suggestive tested leads (T-P01, T-P02). Keep for S11: no partner-runnable program has been tested on Keystone Biology or a comparable high school biology end-of-course exam. Closest leads: Urban Advantage reports some evidence of higher high school science exam passing (T-001); New York Family Rewards and summer jobs report Regents results across subjects (other rows); a Pennsylvania CTE brief (S-0678) is descriptive.
rationale: Honest gap for S11 after this search: nothing a partner could run has been tested on a biology end-of-course exam.

pathway: Teacher absences lower student achievement, and in the United States the levers shown to reduce teacher absence are employer policies (accountability pressure, principals' dismissal authority, tenure timing, leave-pay rules), none of which a partner runs.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: Ten more days of teacher absence lower grade 4 math by about 0.03 standard deviations; accountability pressure and dismissal authority each cut teacher absences by about 10 percent.
caveats: Keep the developing-country review as the only incentive evidence; add that US causal levers are district or state policy. Contrary: Ehrenberg et al. (1991) found teacher absence weakly related to pass rates. A1.3 codes partner staff well-being, not District teachers' attendance.
rationale: Adds US context so the row explains why S2 matters (it moves S5-S8) and why partners cannot claim it. These are associations or policy effects, not partner program models.

evidence_level: gap: no rigorous US study of a staff-support program measured teacher attendance
pathway: Teacher mentoring, mindfulness and wellness programs have not been shown to change teacher attendance; the one strong mindfulness trial did not measure absences and the mentoring study found weak evidence.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
caveats: New York City mentoring (instrumental variables, school fixed effects): weak evidence on absences. CARE for Teachers cluster RCT: absences not reported. Remaining leads are pre-post practicum reports, pre-1990 studies or dissertations (ED324806, EJ386588, ED668403), all below bar.
rationale: Honest gap for S2: a partner offering staff wellness or teacher support has no evidence it moves teacher attendance. Community schools (S-0817) and Urban Advantage (EJ1467585) reduced teacher turnover, which is retention, not attendance.

evidence_level: D (unchanged); add Pennsylvania NOCTI studies and certification-to-graduation evidence
pathway: Technical skills and industry credentials are what the industry skills exam measures; no study tested a partner program's effect on that exam. Earning a certification goes with higher on-time graduation.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: Co-op participants scored higher on NOCTI in an observational Pennsylvania study (size to be confirmed). Florida: certifications raise on-time graduation, more for at-risk students.
caveats: Replace 'the NOCTI exam was never studied' with: the only program-model study with NOCTI as the outcome is an observational Pennsylvania comparison of capstone co-op (T-023), below bar; Staklis & Klein use NOCTI as a predictor (T-024); programs of study raised technical measures in a three-district quasi-experiment run by districts (T-029). For logic models, certification is a cause of S4 (T-025) and college intent but not earnings (T-026).
rationale: Honest gap for S13 stays: nothing a partner runs has been tested against the grade 12 industry certification test. Work-based learning (co-op) is the one partner-adjacent lead and would need a matched study with prior-achievement controls.

pathway: A school-based career-pathway program with employer partners, work-based learning and career counseling did not raise the share of students earning a license or certificate for work.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit. Tested model: Youth CareerConnect (federal grants to high schools with employer partnerships).
typical_effect: Earned a degree, license or certificate for work: not significant (WWC g = -0.06). School attendance rose 0.7 percentage points (S1, out of this screener's scope).
caveats: Credential measure is not the grade 12 industry test; the RCT's credential outcome comes from a student survey in three districts.
rationale: The strongest test of an employer-partner career program on credentials is null: partners acting as employer partners should not claim S13 gains.

proposed_tier: not recommended (context: tested for out-of-school youth)
evidence_level: B-level evidence for a different population
pathway: YouthBuild, run by community organizations, raised the share of out-of-school young people earning a work license or certificate and a diploma or GED.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: YouthBuild (construction or other vocational training, education services, counseling and leadership for low-income 16-24-year-olds without a diploma).
typical_effect: Earned a license or certificate for work g = 0.42 (WWC).
caveats: Population is out of school and aged 16-24, not grade 12 students; credentials are not the CTE industry certification test; diploma results are mostly GED, not four-year graduation.
rationale: The only randomized evidence of a partner-run program raising credential attainment. Listed as context for re-engagement partners; it does not support an S13 claim for in-school youth. Job Corps (S-0313) is a similar federal residential lead, not relied on.
